title: Behavior Problems or Play Deprivation Problems?
author: Kevin Stinehart
summary: Stinehart argues that much of what schools label disruptive behavior is really a symptom of play deprivation. Opening with a student destroying a pencil from restlessness, he reframes dysregulated children as bodies and brains starved of movement and free play, citing Peter Gray and Stuart Brown on the decline of unstructured play. He reports that his school's before- and after-school Play Clubs halved defiance referrals, cut physical aggression from 65 incidents to 32 and ended verbal threats. His case is that regulation is built through experience rather than SEL worksheets or behavior charts, so leaders should ask how much free play a child has had before asking how to secure compliance.
points: Reframes apparent defiance as dysregulation caused by too little movement and unstructured play.
Cites Gray and Brown to claim the prefrontal skills behind self-control develop through child-led play, not lectures.
Reports school data after introducing Play Clubs, with aggression incidents roughly halved, verbal threats at zero and test scores edging up.
Rejects more SEL programs and behavior charts in favor of giving children regulation opportunities.
Challenges teachers and administrators to ask how much free play a child has had and to consider doubling recess.
quotes: The prefrontal cortex, the seat of emotional regulation, focus, impulse control, and empathy doesn’t mature through lectures or lessons. It develops through experiences.

When we cut recess, over-structure the day, or make play something kids earn by complying, we’re not taking away their fun, we’re actually starving their executive function. We are depriving their brains of something they need biologically to be mentally healthy and well.
No rules beyond safety. No adult-directed games or hovering. Just 90 minutes of outdoor freedom after school and 30 minutes before school each day.
You can’t worksheet your way out of what only experience can build. When a child is crying under a table, no behavior chart will reach them.
Over the past five decades or more we have seen a continuous and overall huge decline in children’s freedom to play. With every decade children have become less free to play, roam, and explore.
This wasn’t magic. It was biology. We met their brain’s and bodies’ needs, and their behavior followed…because it finally could.
